title: Foundation self-check
intro: Eight or more questions on modalities, contacts, CIA, reporting, and tiers.

questions.prompt: In S17 and G3, what does Shall mean?
choices: A mandatory requirement. You must do it.
A nice idea for a quiet week.
A suggestion you can ignore if busy.
A vendor marketing claim.
questions.rationale: G3 §4.2: Shall is a mandatory requirement. The same convention is in S17 §4.2.

questions.prompt: What does Should mean in this hub?
choices: Best practice — implement whenever possible.
Optional decoration with no expectation.
A rule that applies only to contractors.
A synonym of May.
questions.rationale: Should is a best practice to implement whenever possible. If you defer it, know why.

questions.prompt: What does May mean?
choices: A desirable best practice.
A mandatory control for every Tier 1 system.
Permission to skip Shall items.
A temporary waiver from DPO.
questions.rationale: May is a desirable best practice. It is not a waiver for Shall.

questions.prompt: What is the reading order for a control?
choices: S17 first, then the same-number G3 section, then App C only if the system is Tier 2 or Tier 3.
App C first, then skip S17 if you are busy.
The practice guide only.
Whatever is shortest.
questions.rationale: Policy (what) before guidelines (how). Appendix C is the extra tier layer, not a replacement.

questions.prompt: Which stack order matches G3 §2.3?
choices: Security Regulations, then S17, then G3, then practice guides, then local B/D policy.
Local habit, then a blog, then S17.
G3 only. S17 is optional.
Appendix C for every Tier 1 PC.
questions.rationale: B/Ds comply with the Security Regulations, S17, and G3, and follow practice guides. Local policy can be stricter.

questions.prompt: Which trio names the core security objectives?
choices: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
Speed, cost, and novelty.
Firewall, antivirus, and password length only.
Classification, colour, and cabinet.
questions.rationale: G3 §4.1 and §6 describe confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Controls serve those objectives.

questions.prompt: A Tier 2 system is best described as:
choices: A system whose failure or disruption would seriously hit government operations, or could cause public turmoil or catastrophe.
Any laptop.
Only a system that is air-gapped.
A system you personally find annoying.
questions.rationale: That is the sense of the G3 §4.1 Tier 2 definition. Tier 3 is a Tier 2 system tied directly to an essential service. Confirm the tier with the owner. Do not self-finalise it.

questions.prompt: When should you report a security event?
choices: When you reasonably see harm to confidentiality, integrity, availability, or operations. Do not wait until you are certain.
Only after a full forensic report.
Only if the Director asks first.
Never, if you can reboot quietly.
questions.rationale: G3 §18 expects prompt reporting. The departmental ISIRT, once aware, phones GIRO Standing Office within 60 minutes and sends the preliminary form within 48 hours. Follow your local procedure.

questions.prompt: Who is the usual departmental lead for IT security accountability?
choices: The Departmental IT Security Officer (DITSO).
The canteen contractor.
Whoever last changed the wallpaper.
GovCERT.HK acting as your line manager.
questions.rationale: G3 §5.2.1 describes the DITSO. You still need the security unit, the ISIRT Commander, and your line manager on the who-to-call card.

questions.prompt: Appendix C applies when:
choices: The system is Tier 2 or Tier 3. Tier 3 also takes every Tier 2 App C control.
The system is any Tier 1 file share.
You feel like reading extra pages.
Only during a penetration test week.
questions.rationale: G3 says B/Ds adopt the baseline for ordinary systems and the stricter Appendix C controls for Tier 2 and Tier 3. Tier 3 includes the Tier 2 App C set.

questions.prompt: Who is the usual departmental lead for IT security accountability?
choices: The Departmental IT Security Officer appointed by the Head of the B/D.
Whoever last opened the firewall ticket.
A supplier’s service desk, by default.
This learning hub.
questions.rationale: S17 §5 and G3 §5 describe the DITSO. You still need the security unit, the ISIRT contact, and your line manager.

questions.prompt: A developer can describe a residual risk. Who accepts what remains?
choices: The management owner, through the department’s own route.
The developer, by merging the code.
The learning-hub checkbox.
No one, if the slide says low.
questions.rationale: S17 §7 and G3 §7 put risk ownership with management. Describing a risk is not the same as accepting it.

questions.prompt: Classified protection means:
choices: Every system, including a shared service, gets a tier and controls to match.
Only Internet-facing systems are in scope.
Tier labels are optional decorations.
The project manager picks Tier 1 to save time.
questions.rationale: S17 §7 treats classification as a management responsibility. Do not finalise a tier to suit a date.

questions.prompt: Departmental policy may be:
choices: Stricter than S17 and G3, and shall not be weaker.
A replacement for S17 if the director prefers it.
Optional reading for administrators.
The only document a new joiner needs.
questions.rationale: S17 §2 and §8 put local policy after the baseline. Local text does not cancel a Shall.

questions.prompt: Which pair is the right reading order for a theme?
choices: S17 first, then the same-theme G3 section.
A blog, then the local habit.
Appendix C for every Tier 1 PC.
G3 only, because it is longer.
questions.rationale: S17 is the mandatory minimum. G3 is the implementation standard for the same theme.

questions.prompt: Your own user duties disappear when a security unit exists.
choices: False. The unit adds specialist duties. Your own Shall items remain.
True. Users only need the poster.
True for developers, false for everyone else.
True once you have attended one briefing.
questions.rationale: S17 §5 and §9 expect every staff member to know their duties. A specialist team does not absorb them.

title: Elevated end user self-check
intro: User and elevated-duty checks, plus one App C point.

questions.prompt: An elevated account you no longer need should be:
choices: Removed or reduced. Access stays justified.
Kept because it was hard to get.
Shared with the whole team for convenience.
Written on a sticky note under the keyboard.
questions.rationale: Least privilege and removal of access are §11 duties. Elevated use may also be audited.

questions.prompt: The access-control principle to remember first is:
choices: Least privilege.
Everyone gets admin on Fridays.
Longer passwords replace all other controls.
Classification labels are optional on RESTRICTED documents.
questions.rationale: G3 §11.1 starts from least privilege. Labels and handling still matter under §10.

questions.prompt: Clear desk and clear screen sit mainly in:
choices: S17/G3 §13 physical and environmental security.
Appendix D filing codes.
The canteen roster.
Section 3 normative references only.
questions.rationale: §13 covers secure areas and equipment habits, including clear desk and clear screen.

questions.prompt: Classified material you need to send should be:
choices: Marked and sent on the channel local rules allow, with encryption when the rule requires it.
Attached to a personal webmail account.
Posted in a team chat with no label.
Copied onto an unlabelled USB “just for the meeting”.
questions.rationale: §15.2 and §12 govern transfer and cryptography. Follow the local rule if it is stricter.

questions.prompt: A suspicious message was opened. Your first learning point is:
choices: Report through the departmental path. Do not wait for a private investigation to finish.
Delete it and hope.
Forward it to friends so they can test the link.
Post screenshots on social media.
questions.rationale: §18: report. A tabletop is for practice. A real event uses the live ISIRT path.

questions.prompt: You administer a task next to a Tier 2 system. Which App C theme applies?
choices: Independent checks of privileged accounts at least every six months, and MFA for interactive privileged logon where feasible.
No extra control, because App C is only for websites.
A public bug-bounty in your own name.
Skipping passwords because MFA exists somewhere else.
questions.rationale: Those are App C §11 controls for Tier 2, and Tier 3 inherits them. Confirm the tier with the owner.

title: System / LAN administrator self-check
intro: Privileged operations, patching, backup, and Tier 3 monitoring.

questions.prompt: A privileged-account inventory is for:
choices: Knowing which powerful accounts exist, why, and who can use them.
A list of favourite passwords in a shared spreadsheet.
Replacing change control.
Publishing admin names on the intranet homepage.
questions.rationale: You cannot review what you have not listed. Pair the inventory with least privilege.

questions.prompt: For a Tier 2 system, how often does App C expect an independent privileged-account check?
choices: At least every six months.
Every five years.
Only after an incident becomes public.
Never, if the same admin reviews their own logins.
questions.rationale: App C §11: an independent party checks privileged use at least every six months. Tier 3 inherits this.

questions.prompt: A known vulnerability has a patch. App C’s usual timing is:
choices: As soon as possible, typically within a month. If it slips, tell the DITSO and keep updating them monthly until it is fixed.
Whenever the next hardware refresh happens.
Only if a newspaper asks.
Within one month, with no need to tell anyone if you miss it.
questions.rationale: App C §14 requires a documented risk view and DITSO visibility when mitigation exceeds a month.

questions.prompt: Tier 2 backup under App C includes:
choices: Local and off-site copies, with the off-site copy kept somewhere secure and remote from the equipment.
One copy on the same disk array.
A screenshot of the backup software.
Backups only after a disaster.
questions.rationale: App C §14 requires local and off-site backup for Tier 2, inherited by Tier 3.

questions.prompt: End-of-support software on a Tier 2 system needs:
choices: A migration plan at least six months before end of support, and the security measures in place by that date.
A note that you will look at it someday.
Nothing, if the vendor still answers email.
An immediate public disclosure of the version.
questions.rationale: That is the App C §14 end-of-support expectation.

questions.prompt: Tier 3 monitoring, beyond the Tier 2 operations controls, means:
choices: 24×7 security surveillance that can correlate multiple sources, of a SIEM class.
A daily glance at one antivirus console.
Monitoring only during office hours.
Disabling logs to save disk.
questions.rationale: App C §14 Tier 3 row: 24×7 monitoring and SIEM-class correlation. Tier 2 controls still apply as well.

title: Application developer self-check
intro: Security in the life cycle, test data, and App C §16.

questions.prompt: Security-by-design means:
choices: Security requirements are in the life cycle from the start, not bolted on at go-live.
A penetration test the night before launch is enough.
Developers skip §16 if a framework is popular.
Production data is the safest test data.
questions.rationale: G3 §6 and §16.1: security is introduced through the development process to avoid late rework.

questions.prompt: For a Tier 2 build, App C §16 expects the pre-production security risk assessment to:
choices: Check that design-review follow-ups were actually implemented before production.
Replace source control.
Be skipped if the sprint is late.
Be done only by the marketing team.
questions.rationale: Shift-left plus that verification is an App C §16 Shall for Tier 2, inherited by Tier 3.

questions.prompt: Hardening before production is used as:
choices: The baseline for later changes.
A one-off screenshot nobody keeps.
A reason to disable logging.
Optional for Internet-facing systems.
questions.rationale: App C §16: harden before rollout, then treat that hardened state as the baseline.

questions.prompt: Production-like test data should be:
choices: Protected, and anonymised where the rule requires it.
Copied to a laptop for the weekend.
Emailed to the whole project alias.
Left in a public bucket so testers can find it.
questions.rationale: G3 §16.3 is about protecting test data that resembles production.

questions.prompt: Where segregation is required, development admin and production admin should be:
choices: Different. Do not reuse production privileges for everyday development.
The same shared account, to save time.
Stored in the README.
Granted to every contractor by default.
questions.rationale: Segregation of duties is a management and build-process expectation. See G3 §7 and §16.2.

questions.prompt: Application secrets belong:
choices: In a controlled secret store, not in source code.
In a comment at the top of the main file.
In the ticket title.
In a screenshot in chat.
questions.rationale: Secrets in source fail both access control and integrity expectations. Treat this as a Shall habit.

title: IT security administrator / unit self-check
intro: Mandate, segregation, reviews, and Tier 3 certification.

questions.prompt: The security administrator and the system administrator should be:
choices: Different persons. The security role should not be the same seat as system administration.
Always the same person, to move faster.
Rotated hourly with a shared password.
Outsourced with no local owner.
questions.rationale: G3 states the security administrator should not also be the system administrator. That protects segregation and log integrity.

questions.prompt: Audit-log integrity means:
choices: The persons under review should not be able to alter the record unnoticed.
Logs can be edited to look tidy.
Logs are optional if the system feels healthy.
Only successful logins are kept.
questions.rationale: Security administrators maintain and review logs. Integrity of that record is part of the job.

questions.prompt: Joiner-mover-leaver is mainly about:
choices: Granting, changing, and removing access as persons change roles.
Ordering laptops only.
A social event.
Skipping §9 because IT is busy.
questions.rationale: §9 and §11 meet here. Leavers and transfers are a common gap.

questions.prompt: An independent privileged-account audit for Tier 2/3 is:
choices: A check by someone other than the account holder, at least every six months.
The admin ticking their own spreadsheet.
Required only for Tier 1 mailboxes.
A public blog post.
questions.rationale: App C §11. Independence is the point.

questions.prompt: A B/D with Tier 3 systems must have, in the security unit:
choices: At least one member with a recognised IT security certification.
No training plan.
Only vendor staff, with no civil-service owner.
A certification wall and nothing else.
questions.rationale: App C §5 names examples such as CISA, CISSP, or CISP. The official text is the list to follow.

questions.prompt: Departmental threat intelligence routes include:
choices: GIRO and GovCERT.HK, plus your local ISIRT path.
Only a personal social-media feed.
Rumours in the lift.
Waiting for a user to notice a defacement.
questions.rationale: G3 §5 describes GIRO and GovCERT.HK. §14.7 is the threat-management theme.

title: Management support self-check
intro: Oversight questions. You are not being trained as the packet analyst.

questions.prompt: The DITSO’s accountability is described in:
choices: G3 §5.2.1 (and the matching S17 section).
The printer manual.
Appendix A sample end-user text only.
A project codename.
questions.rationale: Start oversight reading at the DITSO role, then the steering committee in §5.2.2.

questions.prompt: A B/D that runs Tier 3 systems shall have:
choices: An information security steering committee with senior management and the DITSO, meeting regularly, with outcomes recorded.
A committee only if the budget is leftover.
No documented roles.
A chat channel instead of any record.
questions.rationale: That is the App C §5 Tier 3 organisation control. Tier 2 does not add this particular row, but other Tier 2 App C controls still apply if you also have Tier 2 systems.

questions.prompt: Tier 3 risk registers should at least record:
choices: The risk, likelihood, severity, mitigation, and the monitoring required.
Only the system’s nickname.
A single colour with no owner.
Vendor slogans.
questions.rationale: App C §7 requires the risk-management framework and risk registers for Tier 3 systems.

questions.prompt: Who finalises a Tier 2 or Tier 3 classification?
choices: The Information Owner or DITSO unit confirms it. You do not self-finalise it.
Any developer on the day of go-live.
The hub’s checkbox.
A quiz score.
questions.rationale: G3 §7 requires classification across the life cycle, aligned to the business. This hub only helps you prepare the question.

questions.prompt: A good management question on §11 and §14 is:
choices: Ask the unit for a red/amber/green view of privileged reviews, patch delays, and open assurance items.
Ask for a packet capture in the steering paper.
Ask everyone to share their password to prove access works.
Skip App C because it is an appendix.
questions.rationale: Management support is oversight. Evidence can be a status view. The unit keeps the technical artefacts.

questions.prompt: Appendix D is relevant when:
choices: The system is Tier 2 or Tier 3 and a submission is part of assurance.
You want a shorter password.
The system is a personal phone with no government data.
You are writing a lunch menu.
questions.rationale: Know that Appendix D submissions exist for Tier 2/3 and who in your B/D files them. Do not invent a filing from this hub.

title: App C and tier self-check
intro: Inheritance, which sections carry extra controls, and what you must not decide alone.

questions.prompt: The inheritance rule is:
choices: Tier 3 includes every Tier 2 Appendix C control, plus the Tier 3-only rows.
Tier 3 replaces Tier 2 and drops the Tier 2 rows.
Tier 1 includes Appendix C.
Pick either Tier 2 or Tier 3 rows, not both.
questions.rationale: G3 Appendix C says the Tier 2 controls shall also be adopted by Tier 3 systems.

questions.prompt: Which areas add Tier 3-only organisation, risk, and training controls?
choices: §12 only.
§3 normative references.
None. Appendix C is only about passwords.
questions.rationale: Steering committee and certification are §5. Risk registers are §7. Structured training is §9. They are Tier 3 rows. Other sections still have Tier 2 rows that Tier 3 inherits.

questions.prompt: The privileged-account audit and privileged MFA rules are:
choices: Tier 2 controls, so Tier 3 takes them too.
Tier 3 only, so a Tier 2 system can skip them.
Optional for Internet-facing systems.
Replaced by a longer screensaver.
questions.rationale: They sit in the Tier 2 column of App C §11. Empty Tier 3 cells in that row do not cancel them.

questions.prompt: An Internet-facing Tier 2 system needs penetration testing:
choices: At least once a year, and penetration testing is also part of the security risk assessment for Tier 2.
Never.
Only after a redesign of the logo.
Only if the system is also Tier 3.
questions.rationale: App C §20: pen-test in the SRA for Tier 2, and at least yearly for Internet-facing Tier 2. Tier 3 has a further annual SRA package.

questions.prompt: A Tier 3 security risk assessment under App C includes:
choices: At least an annual assessment, with vulnerability scanning, an independent accredited penetration test, and configuration and source review, endorsed by the DITSO.
A verbal “looks fine”.
A scan once per decade.
A test done only by the developer who wrote the code, with no independence.
questions.rationale: That is the Tier 3 compliance row. Always read the current Appendix C wording before you quote a deadline in a paper.

questions.prompt: You think a system might be Tier 2. What do you do?
choices: Propose the tier with impact, interdependency, and essential-service notes, then confirm with the Information Owner or DITSO unit.
Stamp Tier 3 on the architecture slide yourself.
Ignore Appendix C until an audit.
Treat the hub checkbox as the official classification.
questions.rationale: Classification is a management act under §7. This hub is a learning aid, not the decision.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an empty Tier 2 cell is right?
choices: That area has no extra Tier 2 control in Appendix C. Baseline S17/G3 still applies. Tier 3-only rows do not erase Tier 2 rows elsewhere.
An empty cell means the whole section is optional.
An empty cell means you can skip Shall.
An empty cell downgrades the system to Tier 1.
questions.rationale: Read the matrix by row. Inheritance is across the Tier 2 column, not cancelled by a dash in one cell.

title: Security across the life cycle
intro: Nine stages, from project initiation to decommissioning. Section-level themes only.

questions.prompt: When should the first security requirements be written?
choices: At project initiation and design, while the scope can still change.
The week the system goes live.
After the first incident.
Only if an auditor asks.
questions.rationale: S17 §16 and G3 §16 put security into acquisition and development. S17 §6 calls this security-by-design.

questions.prompt: A supplier will run the system. When do outsourcing duties start?
choices: At procurement, in the agreement, not after an incident.
When the supplier volunteers a slide.
They do not start. Certification replaces the contract.
At decommissioning only.
questions.rationale: S17 §17 and G3 §17 keep the B/D responsible. The contract has to say what the supplier still owes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about go-live is right?
choices: Open Shall gaps need an owner, and the incident route has to be known.
A successful demo closes every Shall.
Tier can be chosen after go-live to reduce work.
Backup can be designed the following quarter.
questions.rationale: Go-live checks the §14 and §16 baseline and §18 readiness. An unowned Shall gap is not accepted by silence.

questions.prompt: A major change to a live system should prompt you to ask:
choices: Whether requirements, the tier, or the security risk assessment need to be reopened.
Only whether the colour of the logo changed.
Nothing, if the change is by a vendor.
Whether you can skip access control this once.
questions.rationale: S17 §14, §16, and §20 treat change as a point where assurance can be needed again.

questions.prompt: Decommissioning includes:
choices: Removing access and sanitising or returning media and supplier-held data.
Turning the server off and hoping the backups expire.
Keeping privileged accounts for nostalgia.
Posting the data to a personal drive first.
questions.rationale: S17 §10, §11, and §17 cover disposal, access removal, and the end of a supplier’s copy.

questions.prompt: The nine stages in this hub run in which order?
choices: Initiation, design, procurement, build, testing, go-live, operations, change, decommissioning.
Go-live, then requirements, then a tier sticker.
Procurement, then incident response, then design.
There is no order. Pick the shortest page.
questions.rationale: The hub uses those nine names so current staff can filter by the stage they are actually in.

title: Incident reporting
intro: Clear the common misconceptions about when to report and who to tell.

questions.prompt: When should you report a security event?
choices: When harm to confidentiality, integrity, availability, or operations is reasonably apparent. Do not wait until you are certain.
Only after a full forensic report.
Only if you can name the attacker.
Never, if a reboot might hide it.
questions.rationale: S17 §18 and G3 §18 expect prompt reporting. Certainty is not the threshold.

questions.prompt: Who do you tell first?
choices: Your departmental route: line manager and the incident contact on the who-to-call card.
A wide team chat, with the suspicious attachment.
A personal social-media account.
No one, until the Director emails you.
questions.rationale: The departmental ISIRT runs the central clocks once they are aware. You use the local route. Do not invent a phone number.

questions.prompt: You clicked a suspicious link and nothing obvious happened. You should:
choices: Report it and say what you clicked.
Wait a week to see if you feel sure.
Delete every log so the desk looks tidy, then report.
Forward the lure to the whole unit.
questions.rationale: Possible harm is enough to report. Do not destroy the timeline first, and do not spread the lure.

questions.prompt: A drill for practice should be:
choices: Labelled as a drill, with fake data, and kept off the real incident path.
A real phishing message sent to colleagues.
An unauthorised scan of a production system.
Posted as if it were a live GIRO report.
questions.rationale: Practice stays a drill. A real event uses the real procedure.

questions.prompt: There is no Appendix C block on incident management. That means:
choices: The S17 §18 and G3 §18 baseline still applies at every tier.
Tier 2 systems need not report incidents.
Only Tier 3 systems report incidents.
Incident reporting is a May.
questions.rationale: No Appendix C block does not delete the baseline. Reporting remains a Shall.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the first note?
choices: What happened, when, which system, and what you do not yet know.
A guess at the attacker’s name presented as fact.
Passwords, so the handler can log in as you.
Nothing. Speech is enough and no one writes it down.
questions.rationale: G3 §18 and the local procedure say what to preserve. Unknown is an acceptable fact. Leave secrets out of the note.
